Why does this feel so scary? 😂

It’s actually crazy to think that anxiety can go through the roof if we leave the house without headphones.

Trust me, I’ve been there.

Like literal panic if I’ve stepped in the gym and can’t find headphones.

Or for some reason Apple CarPlay doesn’t connect when you step in the car 🤦🏻‍♂️ 

I honestly get that we’re all living suuuuuper busy lives.

And trying to knock two birds with one stone by listening to music or podcasts whilst running, working out or driving feels like a no-brainer…

But I’ve actually found that it kind of works as a distraction in the moment.

Especially if you’re trying to get rid of stress.

But it doesn’t make it go away.

The BEST way to give your brain room to process, reflect and reset.

I’m sorry…

But it’s to de-stimulate.

No music. No podcasts. No audiobooks.

Try it for like ONE day a week and see what happens to your mental clarity.

#Productivity #Overstimulated #Podcast #Workout #Calm

Some journal prompts to help build the skill of metacognition below: 

• What’s one thought my mind constantly loops back to when I’m  tired or stressed?

• Is that negative thought actually true, or is my brain just making it up?

• Did I  make my last big decision based on facts, or just how I felt in the moment?

• What exact feeling am I  trying to escape the second i pick up your phone to distract myself?

. What’s a positive and useful thought pattern I have about myself? 

If I spoke to my friends the way I talk to myself in my head, would they still be my friends?

Do my thoughts usually spiral into the past (regret), the future (anxiety), or stay right here?

Try these out in a journal! Hand write them 👏👏

Up 4-1 at the WTA Finals, Aryna Sabalenka lost 11 straight games. Asked what she'd tell herself as her own coach, she gave the answer most of us think, then the one most of us need.

The devil always gets the first word. It doesn't have to get the last.

Our inner voice acts as a safety mechanism, translating our inner world into something we can process and deal with… We may feel stress or anxiety, but we have limited options to deal with the sensation. As Fernyhough argues, “If negative emotions are channeled into the auditory modality, it might make them slightly easier to deal with. Voices and negative rumination might be unpleasant, but at least they can be engaged with. In which case, the dominance of inner speech might ultimately reflect its evolved role in making the organism resilient to stress.”

Voices allow us to do something about what we feel. To actively engage and negotiate… We go from being able only to ignore or embrace to being able to negotiate, create distance and space from, or simply brush off as a self not worth listening to.

-Steve

Dribble running is a staple in my programs for a few reasons.

A lot of GAA players lack stiffness and reactivity through the ankle, knee, hip and trunk at higher speeds.

They plod into the ground and keep pushing long after they should be off it.

Acceleration is force-dominant. Longer ground contacts help you overcome inertia and build up speed initially. This is favourable.

Upright running and top speed are different.

You need to be reactive, bouncy and stiff up the chain. Attack the floor, get back off it fast and prepare quickly for the next contact. 

When you become an overpusher, everything happens behind you. Backside mechanics aren’t automatically bad, but living there makes it harder to recover the leg and punch the knee through for the next stride.

At higher speeds this can:

* Limit your top-speed ceiling
* overextend the lower back
* Increase the demand on your calves, hamstrings and quads (strains)
* Contribute to the same niggles continually appearing

It isn’t the sole reason players get injured, but it can absolutely be a contributing factor.

This is why I use constraints in movement prep and dribble running.

Not just to make a drill look good, but to help the athlete find better stiffness, quicker contacts and more efficient front-side mechanics.

Inside 365, we work on both sides of running:

Force and projection for acceleration.

Stiffness and reactivity for upright running and top speed.

The off-season is where you actually get the time to build these qualities before you’re expected to express them every weekend in games.

This doesn’t mean you turn into a ‘perfect’ runner. Everyone moves differently and not everyone needs to completely change how they move.

But from a high speed running perspective, frontside mechanics are favourable.

Stacking weeks of training matters. But so does stopping to check whether the work is actually moving you forward.

The off-season is your biggest opportunity to raise your physical ceiling, but only if you train with real structure, intent and accountability. Random sessions and a generic club gym plan that you half arse won’t do that.

latestPosts.caption:
Game conditioning works, but it isn’t always the best way to actually build your engine.

GAA is repeated high-intensity efforts with incomplete recovery. That demands all three energy systems - but most players don’t train any to a high level.

Or they just run until they’re cooked and call it ‘conditioning’.

This is the framework I use to build those systems with my 365 athletes, both on and off feet 👇

AEROBIC: BUILD THE FOUNDATION

Your aerobic system helps rebuild explosive energy between efforts. Improve it and the drop-off from your first sprint to your last gets smaller.

Examples:

Aerobic capacity: 45 minutes steady on the bike at Zone 2 - approximately 60–70% max HR or RPE 3–5
Aerobic power: Norwegian 4 × 4 at approximately 90–95% max HR, a favourite of mine 

ANAEROBIC GLYCOLYTIC: PRODUCE IN THE RED ZONE

This supports you when the intensity is too high for aerobic energy production to meet the full demand.

It’s useful but it comes with a high fatigue cost. Use it strategically rather than trying to bury yourself every week. I use off feet to target this in the off season

ALACTIC: SPEED AND EXPLOSIVE POWER

Short, maximal-intent efforts with long recovery.

Accelerations. Flying 15s. Maximum-speed running. Real quality while you’re fresh and ready to go with intent.

Then you have to fit it into an actual week.

High days high. Low days low.

Sitting in the moderately hard middle every day creates fatigue without developing any one quality properly.

A five-minute maximum run gives you a useful MAS estimate. GPS or timing gates tell you your top speed. Retest every five weeks and find out whether the programme is actually working.

Every session needs a clear focus:

What quality are we targeting - and are you bringing enough intent to create the adaptation?

Save this for your next conditioning block. Send it to the teammate who thinks conditioning means running until you’re sick

This is probably the most personal post I’ve ever shared on here, 6 years later 😅 

The truth is there was never some master plan to build The 365 Athlete to where it is now.

It started with a chubby kid who was completely obsessed with GAA - but couldn’t make school teams and couldn’t understand why he wasn’t good enough.

Getting overlooked hurt me a lot even at such a young age. For years, that hurt became fuel.

I trained relentlessly from the age of 15. I changed myself physically. I went from sitting on the bench to playing county football within a few years.

For a while I thought hard work was the answer to everything, until I eventually broke down 

I trained harder, optimised everything and went down every avenue possible - only to end up injured, frustrated and completely lost.

That period humbled me big time😅

But it also forced me to accept that effort without direction only takes you so far. That athletes don’t just need another program, they need education, structure, guidance, community - and someone in their corner who genuinely gives a fck.

So I went searching for better answers.

I learned. I experimented. I made mistakes. I invested in coaches and mentors, and still do. I applied everything to myself and eventually began helping other GAA players do the same.

That became The 365 Athlete. A thriving community of athletes who all want to leave their jerseys in a better place. 

Over 1,000 players have now come through my programmes, which still feels mental to write.

But I haven’t got everything figured out.

I’m still playing and still learning. Still getting things wrong. Still trying to become the athlete, coach and man I know I can be.

365 exists because I wanted to build what the younger me desperately needed 10 years ago.

A place for ambitious GAA players who don’t want to leave their potential unexplored.

I’m building it for that kid and for every athlete who feels like him now. 

Purpose. Preparation. Performance.

365.

Not everyone I coach has a GPS and so plenty of others have got faster and feel way better on the pitch without ever having a number to show for it. And although data is cool, how they feel is the part I go to most. But where we can measure it, the numbers back it up.

I’ve spent years building the 365 system, and this is what it comes down to 👇🏻

Speed work, every week. Max velocity, acceleration, change of direction and agility, trained properly and consistently. No excuses.

The prep work before every speed session. Executed to a high level. 

How you move in the gym. Feeling the positions you need to be in to put force into the floor quickly. Improving co-ordination so force is applied efficiently.

Posture. Better posture puts you in a better position to apply force. There’s no point being strong as fck if you can’t apply it.

The numbers are the part you can see. The rest is unseen work: positions, posture and coordination, so that you can actually use the strength you have. That’s what makes the biggest difference.

Recovery can’t rescue bad programming.

You can sleep eight hours, nail your nutrition, go for walks, stretch, cold plunge and buy every recovery tool under the sun, but if you consistently demand more from your body than it has the capacity to tolerate, you’re still going to feel absolutely cooked.

Recovery isn’t something you hack unfortunately, it’s the relationship between the work you’re doing and the work you’re currently capable of recovering from.

There will be periods where we deliberately push beyond that capacity to create an adaptation. But that should be planned, controlled and followed by an opportunity to recover - not repeated blindly until your body fails you.

The day-to-day fundamentals are boring:

Sleep enough.
Eat enough.
Consume adequate protein and carbohydrates.
Reduce stress where possible.
And sometimes, genuinely do fck all.

But the long-term answer is to build a bigger capacity for work.

More strength work, executed properly.
A bigger aerobic engine.
Greater exposure to speed, acceleration, deceleration and change of direction.
All progressed gradually through a properly structured week.

That’s what the off-season is for.

Because your ability to recover when the games and training loads go through the roof next summer is being built right now.

Do the work.

A new programme won’t fix an old standard - think about that for a second.

A lot of athletes keep searching for the perfect plan, coach or system to transform them.

But the harder question is 👇🏻

Have you ever fully committed to one with a growth oriented mindset? 

Inside 365, our responsibility is to provide the structure, programming, education, feedback and support - and to help you adapt it when your club schedule, injury or circumstances change.

We own that responsibility completely.

But we cannot complete the sessions for you. We cannot prepare your food, prioritise your sleep, communicate on your behalf or maintain your standards when motivation drops.

You have to own that.

This isn’t about blaming athletes or pretending every programme is perfect, sometimes genuine circumstances get in the way. It’s about understanding that coaching is a partnership.

The athletes who achieve the most inside 365 ask questions. They communicate when they’re struggling. They use the support and education available. But ultimately, they take responsibility for their own progress. From there the sky is the limit.

If you want someone to chase and carry you every day, 365 probably isn’t the right environment for you.

If you want a proven system, high standards and a group that will support you while you take ownership of becoming a better athlete, applications are open through the link in my bio. The standard of athlete who can get in is going up, I make no apologies for that. 

I personally review every application and select the athletes I believe are genuinely ready for it.

latestPosts.caption:
A diary entry from a week in Lagos 🇵🇹

As athletes we spend so much of the year in attack mode.

Training and competing, then trying to recover. Optimising everything we do, or at least trying to. Setting high standards and constantly looking for the next 1%.

That’s a massive part of what it takes to perform, but it also comes at a heavy enough cost physically and mentally.

High performance needs periods where none of that matters as well

Periods of stillness. Of simply experiencing life and allowing your body and mind to recharge 

That was this week for me in Lagos before the event.

I didn’t bring any of the gadgets or supplements I would normally take away. I trained twice with no real structure.

Most days were spent on the beach doing Sudoku and having the craic. We walked along the coast from Lagos at sunrise - just taking in some insane views which was cool.

Most days we had couple of beers before dinner while playing cards. Early nights and early mornings for sunrise (elite). Some of the best croissants I’ve had in my life, coffees and eating whatever I fancied without analysing the calories or wondering whether I’d eaten enough protein.

For a few days, I dropped the need to be optimal (one mode I used to badly struggle with)

There was no guilt about doing less because I had intentionally lowered my expectations for the week. 

I did things purely for fun and it might genuinely be the best I’ve ever switched off on a trip away. I think that’s what actual rest is as an athlete.

Not lying around while your head is still racing with everything you should be doing. Actually giving yourself permission to stop everything and be in the now.

To be present and to fully experience whatever it is you’re doing,

Because high performance doesn’t only require the ability to push like a lunatic year round.

It also requires knowing when to completely let go.

The batteries feel full again.

At the same time though, looking forward to going full attack mode again as an athlete and business owner.

A week well spent with great company 🫡

I asked @jakobing how a recreational runner can become stronger, healthier and happier. His answer: “I would focus on a routine. I would try to build a routine and making things consistently and sustainable. And also having a goal in mind.” 
After interviewing hundreds of World Class athletes, coaches and experts I often hear the same words: consistency, routines, habits and patience. 

That’s the whole idea behind BACK TO BASICS 30, a 30-day Accountability Challenge inside my Personal Best Running Coaching Program starting September 1st.   For 30 days, we focus on four simple fundamentals: daily movement, consistent quality sleep, clean nutrition, and some type of daily strength training. Nothing extreme. Just showing up for the basics, with a customizable habit tracker to keep you on track, daily guidance from me, and a community holding each other accountable.

A few questions I’ve been getting:

What if I’m mid-training-cycle for a fall race? Still works. You decide what each fundamental looks like for you, so it fits around your existing plan instead of replacing it.

What if I’m just getting back into running after time off? Also works. This isn’t a training plan, it’s an accountability layer under whatever you’re already doing, whether that’s starting from zero or deep in marathon prep.

How much time does this take? Not much. It’s four areas you’re probably already thinking about, just approached with more intention.

Is this part of the Personal Best Program? Yes, it’s included with a PB Program membership, along with 30+ training plans, video library, weekly live coaching, and daily support from me, other PB coaches and the community.

Starts September 1st. Link in bio to join.

Recently I sat down with @jakobing, one of the greatest middle-distance runners of all time, Olympic champion in the 1500m and 5000m, and multi-time world champion.

One thing that blew my mind is how extremely hard he trains and recovers.

Jakob described 14 runs per week: • 8 low intensity runs • 6 high intensity workouts • 5 workouts around 4 mmol blood lactate • 1 workout around 8–10 mmol

He mentioned “Threshold Fever,” training so hard that between sessions your body is working so intensely that all you can do is lie on the couch and recover.

As Jakob put it: “If you’re able to study or work, you’re not fatigued enough.” 😅

At the same time, he shared many lessons that everyday runners can apply too:

“I recommend people to have fun, but also finding a rhythm that works. And once you get into that rhythm, it’s easier to improve.”

“You can’t fear the consequences of not making it. You have to have an open mind and be prepared to face the challenges.”

“If you overdo it, it’s not sustainable. And if you underdo it, you’re not maximizing the potential.”

“You can’t pull the carrot from the ground to check if it’s growing. You have to believe in the process and wait until it’s finished.”

“It’s very easy to be confident because I can just tell myself, ‘I’ve done this thousand times.’”

“I would focus on a routine. I would try to build a routine and make things consistently and sustainable.”

“Today’s Friday is most likely the same training as last Friday. And that makes it just a little bit easier to make sure that you’re doing the right thing.”

“By just slightly improving every day in training, in 10 to 15 years you are going to improve.”

Full episode is available on YouTube and all podcast platforms. Link in my bio @florisgierman

Day 24. Lessen the noise. The perfect workout is one you can actually stick with and progress.

Of course this is only from a running economy performance lens. If you have genuine injury history or imbalances that need to be worked on and your physio has given you exercises to address these you should still do those.

But I think for a lot of runners if you’re not doing any exercise in the gym by just implementing these principals and keeping it simple you’ll remove a lot of the uncertainty of what to actually do.

During my last marathon block I genuinely just did twice per week:

- heavy Bulgarian splits squats
- heavy single leg RDLs
- heavy isometric calf raises
- isometric Copenhagen holds

And that was it. Progressed over time and got stronger as the block went on and then tapered it down. Never felt like it was interfering with my running.

Day 23. Apologies to the parents out there on this one, but it turns out good sleep makes a big difference to running performance. 

The research is pretty convincing:

• Sleep deprivation has a moderate negative effect on endurance performance, particularly as exercise duration increases.

• In one study, extending sleep to ~8+ hours for just three nights improved endurance time-trial performance, while restricting sleep to ~5 hours made it worse.

• Across studies in athletes, sleep extension and napping are among the most effective sleep interventions for improving subsequent physical and cognitive performance.

The interesting bit for runners isn’t just whether a bad night’s sleep makes tomorrow’s run slower.

It’s what happens when you consistently sleep well enough to turn up ready to perform, recover and repeat good training week after week.

Training is the stimulus. Sleep is part of what allows you to actually benefit from it.

I had the best day on the best day to be in the best city in the world.

Can’t imagine a more meaningful way to mark my new relationship with running than to serve as run support for former Army Master Sergeant @cedrickingmsg — a purple-hearted double above-the-knee amputee due to stepping on an IED.

A victory for me to just make it to the start, crossing the finish with Cedric was a peak never-will-I-forget life experience.

Rewinding back a year and half, my spine surgeon said I should forget about running. Forget that, I thought. So, I baked up a plan and began plotting my way in. 

For the first seven months of my spinal fusion recovery, only slow walking. I began PT on month 8, with light strength training starting a few weeks after that.

Since then, I’ve been in my home gym by the four o’clock hour, every single day aside from a handful of exceptions.

To celebrate 1 year post-op, I ran my first mile, a slow one with @dan_churchill. From there, I patiently pursued a six-month relationship with my treadmill, careful to never push with a first-for-me less-is-best philosophy.

As a consequence of caution, I can’t say I was exactly ready for the NYC marathon, as my run training consisted of two weekly 5-mile run-walks.

Nevertheless, I decided to give it a go. And I’m delighted I did. The spine did fine. And despite my lack of aerobic conditioning, my body held up long enough to cross the finish line.

Striding alongside Cedric is the how. Taking my strength from his kept me connected to my higher power.

The why. While running again was my goal, Cedric confirmed that my purpose is service.

Now 60 and now on the other side of my season of forced repose, I have greater clarity on what matters. Not so much about ego gratification anymore, what wakes me up is more giving of myself to other people. 

If you want a big and beautiful life, make it about something much larger than yourself.

Thx @achilles_international for your incredible work. @joechura for recruiting me into this adventure & @cedrickingmsg for your strength, and infectious inspiration.

And thank you NYC. You remain undefeated.  You leave me hopeful. 

See you next year.
❤️ -r

Almost 10 years between these 2 times.
23 years old vs 32 years old.
The journey 👇🏻
.
.
First ever 5k: 25:14
👉🏻 5 years later I broke 17 minutes
👉🏻 4 years later I broke 15 minutes 
.
When it comes to endurance running it’s the journey that counts.
There is no finish line.
Stacking brick after brick after brick is the win! 🧱 
.
Goals keep you motivated 🎯 
PBs get you high on life and are so rewarding!
.
But it’s that mentally of chasing mini goal after mini goal, that is the best thing to come out of it all.
.
There are no shortcuts.
There are no secrets.
If you relentlessly show up, consistently, over a period of time. Then I promise you, you will surprise yourself!
.
My structure hasn’t changed much at all.
2 and a half harder days in a week and the rest eeezy. So;
1x Track/interval sesh (VO2 Max)
1x Tempo/threshold or hill sesh (comfortably working)
1x Long run (honest work)
The rest eeezy.
.

I don’t have many pics from my early running days.
